For Georgia debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Georgia debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Georgia Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student-loan adversary proceedings under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8) are filed inside an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Georgia consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the universe of cases where an adversary could have been brought.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,240 bankruptcy cases from Georgia's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 796998.6%0.8%

Chapter 1327171.2%28.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Partial Discharge in Georgia

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In Georgia, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for Georgia Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every Georgia debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness - up to $17,500 for qualifying teachers in low-income schools after five years.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

Georgia Legal Aid and Clinic Resources

Atlanta Legal Aid; Georgia Legal Services Program; 11th Circuit Cox governs.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in Georgia can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope; dischargeable without undue-hardship showing.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative; the 8th Circuit rejected the rigid Brunner three-prong framework.

## Brunner Test in Hawaii [2026]: Ninth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/hawaii.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Hawaii [2026]: Ninth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Hawaii residents.

Undue Hardship in Hawaii

Hawaii is in the 9th Circuit, which applies Brunner with the Pena gloss (In re Pena, 155 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 1998)). Partial discharges are available and the DOJ/DOE November 2022 attestation guidance is well-integrated into practice.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Hawaii debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner with Pena gloss framework described below.

The Ninth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner with the Pena gloss. In re Pena, 155 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 1998). Partial discharges and DOJ/DOE Nov 2022 guidance well-integrated into practice.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in Hawaii, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling Hawaii cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Private Student Loans and Hawaii - The McDaniel Question

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8)(B). Loans that were not used solely for "qualified higher education expenses" - including living expenses beyond the cost of attendance, bar study loans, test prep loans, and some direct-to-consumer private loans - may fall outside Section 523(a)(8)(B) entirely and be dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

For Hawaii debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in Hawaii have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For Hawaii debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Hawaii debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Partial Discharge in Hawaii

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In Hawaii, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for Hawaii Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every Hawaii debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness - up to $17,500 for qualifying teachers in low-income schools after five years.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

Hawaii Legal Aid and Clinic Resources

Legal Aid Society of Hawaii; 9th Circuit Pena permits partial discharge.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in Hawaii can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in Indiana, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling Indiana cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Private Student Loans and Indiana - The McDaniel Question

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8)(B). Loans that were not used solely for "qualified higher education expenses" - including living expenses beyond the cost of attendance, bar study loans, test prep loans, and some direct-to-consumer private loans - may fall outside Section 523(a)(8)(B) entirely and be dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

For Indiana debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in Indiana have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For Indiana debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Indiana debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Indiana Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student-loan adversary proceedings under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8) are filed inside an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Indiana consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the universe of cases where an adversary could have been brought.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 3,325 bankruptcy cases from Indiana's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 779297.5%2.0%

Chapter 132,53369.8%29.5%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Partial Discharge in Indiana

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In Indiana, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for Indiana Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every Indiana debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness - up to $17,500 for qualifying teachers in low-income schools after five years.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

Indiana Legal Aid and Clinic Resources

Indiana Legal Services; 7th Circuit framework applies.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in Indiana can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope; dischargeable without undue-hardship showing.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative; the 8th Circuit rejected the rigid Brunner three-prong framework.

## Brunner Test in Iowa [2026]: Eighth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/iowa.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Iowa [2026]: Eighth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Iowa residents.

Undue Hardship in Iowa

Iowa is in the 8th Circuit, which does NOT apply the Brunner test. Instead, the 8th Circuit uses a totality-of-the-circumstances test under Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003). Courts weigh past, present, and future financial resources, reasonable living expenses, and any other relevant facts - with no rigid three-prong structure.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Iowa debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the totality-of-the-circumstances framework described below.

The Eighth Circuit Framework

Does NOT apply Brunner. Uses the totality-of-the-circumstances test. Long v. Educational Credit Management Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003); ECMC v. Jesperson, 571 F.3d 775 (8th Cir. 2009). Structurally more debtor-friendly.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Iowa debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

In Iowa, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

## Brunner Test in Kansas [2026]: Tenth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/kansas.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Kansas [2026]: Tenth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Kansas residents.

Undue Hardship in Kansas

Kansas is in the Tenth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding filed under Bankruptcy Rule 7001.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Kansas debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner three-prong framework described below.

The Tenth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner. In re Woodcock, 45 F.3d 363 (10th Cir. 1995). The McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) decision narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) - important for private loan dischargeability.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

## Brunner Test in Louisiana [2026]: Fifth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/louisiana.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Louisiana [2026]: Fifth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Louisiana residents.

Undue Hardship in Louisiana

Louisiana is in the Fifth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding filed under Bankruptcy Rule 7001.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Louisiana debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner three-prong framework described below.

The Fifth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner. In re Gerhardt, 348 F.3d 89 (5th Cir. 2003). Historically strict; Thomas (2019) narrowed "minimal standard of living" while reaffirming the basic framework.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in Louisiana, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling Louisiana cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Private Student Loans and Louisiana - The McDaniel Question

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8)(B). Loans that were not used solely for "qualified higher education expenses" - including living expenses beyond the cost of attendance, bar study loans, test prep loans, and some direct-to-consumer private loans - may fall outside Section 523(a)(8)(B) entirely and be dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

For Louisiana debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in Louisiana have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For Louisiana debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Louisiana debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Partial Discharge in Louisiana

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In Louisiana, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for Louisiana Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every Louisiana debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness - up to $17,500 for qualifying teachers in low-income schools after five years.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

Louisiana Legal Aid and Clinic Resources

Southeast Louisiana Legal Services; Acadiana Legal Service; 5th Circuit strict Brunner.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in Louisiana can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope; dischargeable without undue-hardship showing.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative; the 8th Circuit rejected the rigid Brunner three-prong framework.

## Brunner Test in Maine [2026]: First Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/maine.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Maine [2026]: First Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Maine residents.

Undue Hardship in Maine

Maine is in the 1st Circuit, which blends Brunner with totality-of-the-circumstances flexibility. The three-prong framework supplies structure but courts retain equitable discretion on the "additional circumstances" prong.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Maine debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the blended Brunner framework described below.

The First Circuit Framework

Blends Brunner with totality-of-circumstances flexibility. Bronsdon v. ECMC, 435 B.R. 791 (1st Cir. BAP 2010); In re Nash, 446 F.3d 188 (1st Cir. 2006). Partial discharge and equitable considerations are comparatively accessible.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

In Maine, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

## Brunner Test in Maryland [2026]: Fourth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/maryland.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Maryland [2026]: Fourth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Maryland residents.

Undue Hardship in Maryland

Maryland is in the Fourth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding filed under Bankruptcy Rule 7001.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Maryland debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner three-prong framework described below.

The Fourth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner strictly. In re Frushour, 433 F.3d 393 (4th Cir. 2005). Good-faith inquiry expects documented IBR/IDR attempts and payment efforts.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Maryland debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

## Brunner Test in Michigan [2026]: Sixth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/michigan.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Michigan [2026]: Sixth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Michigan residents.

Undue Hardship in Michigan

Michigan is in the Sixth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding filed under Bankruptcy Rule 7001.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Michigan debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner three-prong framework described below.

The Sixth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner. In re Oyler, 397 F.3d 382 (6th Cir. 2005). Good-faith evaluated against repayment history and lifestyle choices.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in Michigan, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling Michigan cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Private Student Loans and Michigan - The McDaniel Question

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8)(B). Loans that were not used solely for "qualified higher education expenses" - including living expenses beyond the cost of attendance, bar study loans, test prep loans, and some direct-to-consumer private loans - may fall outside Section 523(a)(8)(B) entirely and be dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

For Michigan debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in Michigan have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For Michigan debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Michigan debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Michigan Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student-loan adversary proceedings under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8) are filed inside an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Michigan consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the universe of cases where an adversary could have been brought.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,133 bankruptcy cases from Michigan's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7633100.0%0.0%

Chapter 1350048.3%51.0%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Partial Discharge in Michigan

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In Michigan, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for Michigan Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every Michigan debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness - up to $17,500 for qualifying teachers in low-income schools after five years.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

Michigan Legal Aid and Clinic Resources

Legal Aid of Western Michigan; Michigan Legal Help; 6th Circuit framework.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in Michigan can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope; dischargeable without undue-hardship showing.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative; the 8th Circuit rejected the rigid Brunner three-prong framework.

## Brunner Test in Minnesota [2026]: Eighth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/minnesota.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Minnesota [2026]: Eighth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Minnesota residents.

Undue Hardship in Minnesota

Minnesota is in the 8th Circuit, which does NOT apply the Brunner test. Instead, the 8th Circuit uses a totality-of-the-circumstances test under Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003). Courts weigh past, present, and future financial resources, reasonable living expenses, and any other relevant facts - with no rigid three-prong structure.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Minnesota debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the totality-of-the-circumstances framework described below.

The Eighth Circuit Framework

Does NOT apply Brunner. Uses the totality-of-the-circumstances test. Long v. Educational Credit Management Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003); ECMC v. Jesperson, 571 F.3d 775 (8th Cir. 2009). Structurally more debtor-friendly.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/montana.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Montana [2026]: Ninth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Montana residents.

Undue Hardship in Montana

Montana is in the 9th Circuit, which applies Brunner with the Pena gloss (In re Pena, 155 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 1998)). Partial discharges are available and the DOJ/DOE November 2022 attestation guidance is well-integrated into practice.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Montana debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner with Pena gloss framework described below.

The Ninth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner with the Pena gloss. In re Pena, 155 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 1998). Partial discharges and DOJ/DOE Nov 2022 guidance well-integrated into practice.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in Montana, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling Montana cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Private Student Loans and Montana - The McDaniel Question

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8)(B). Loans that were not used solely for "qualified higher education expenses" - including living expenses beyond the cost of attendance, bar study loans, test prep loans, and some direct-to-consumer private loans - may fall outside Section 523(a)(8)(B) entirely and be dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

For Montana debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in Montana have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For Montana debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Montana debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Partial Discharge in Montana

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In Montana, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for Montana Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every Montana debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness - up to $17,500 for qualifying teachers in low-income schools after five years.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

Montana Legal Aid and Clinic Resources

Montana Legal Services Association; 9th Circuit Pena.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in Montana can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope; dischargeable without undue-hardship showing.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative; the 8th Circuit rejected the rigid Brunner three-prong framework.

## Brunner Test in Nebraska [2026]: Eighth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/nebraska.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Nebraska [2026]: Eighth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Nebraska residents.

Undue Hardship in Nebraska

Nebraska is in the 8th Circuit, which does NOT apply the Brunner test. Instead, the 8th Circuit uses a totality-of-the-circumstances test under Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003). Courts weigh past, present, and future financial resources, reasonable living expenses, and any other relevant facts - with no rigid three-prong structure.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Nebraska debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the totality-of-the-circumstances framework described below.

The Eighth Circuit Framework

Does NOT apply Brunner. Uses the totality-of-the-circumstances test. Long v. Educational Credit Management Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003); ECMC v. Jesperson, 571 F.3d 775 (8th Cir. 2009). Structurally more debtor-friendly.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in Nebraska, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling Nebraska cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Nebraska debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

## Brunner Test in New Hampshire [2026]: First Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/new-hampshire.html

Brunner Test in New Hampshire [2026]: First Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Hampshire residents.

Undue Hardship in New Hampshire

New Hampshire is in the 1st Circuit, which blends Brunner with totality-of-the-circumstances flexibility. The three-prong framework supplies structure but courts retain equitable discretion on the "additional circumstances" prong.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A New Hampshire debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the blended Brunner framework described below.

The First Circuit Framework

Blends Brunner with totality-of-circumstances flexibility. Bronsdon v. ECMC, 435 B.R. 791 (1st Cir. BAP 2010); In re Nash, 446 F.3d 188 (1st Cir. 2006). Partial discharge and equitable considerations are comparatively accessible.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

## Brunner Test in New Jersey [2026]: Third Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/new-jersey.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in New Jersey [2026]: Third Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Jersey residents.

Undue Hardship in New Jersey

New Jersey is in the Third Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding filed under Bankruptcy Rule 7001.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A New Jersey debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner three-prong framework described below.

The Third Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner. In re Faish, 72 F.3d 298 (3d Cir. 1995). Some bankruptcy courts in the circuit permit partial discharge using Saxman-style reasoning.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in New Jersey, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling New Jersey cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Private Student Loans and New Jersey - The McDaniel Question

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8)(B). Loans that were not used solely for "qualified higher education expenses" - including living expenses beyond the cost of attendance, bar study loans, test prep loans, and some direct-to-consumer private loans - may fall outside Section 523(a)(8)(B) entirely and be dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

For New Jersey debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in New Jersey have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For New Jersey debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A New Jersey debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

New Jersey Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student-loan adversary proceedings under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8) are filed inside an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The New Jersey consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the universe of cases where an adversary could have been brought.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,580 bankruptcy cases from New Jersey's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 752697.3%2.7%

Chapter 131,05431.0%68.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Partial Discharge in New Jersey

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In New Jersey, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for New Jersey Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every New Jersey debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness - up to $17,500 for qualifying teachers in low-income schools after five years.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

New Jersey Legal Aid and Clinic Resources

Legal Services of New Jersey; Volunteer Lawyers for Justice; 3rd Circuit Faish.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in New Jersey can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope; dischargeable without undue-hardship showing.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative; the 8th Circuit rejected the rigid Brunner three-prong framework.

## Brunner Test in New Mexico [2026]: Tenth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

Brunner Test in New Mexico [2026]: Tenth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Mexico residents.

Undue Hardship in New Mexico

New Mexico is in the Tenth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding filed under Bankruptcy Rule 7001.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A New Mexico debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner three-prong framework described below.

The Tenth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner. In re Woodcock, 45 F.3d 363 (10th Cir. 1995). The McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) decision narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) - important for private loan dischargeability.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling New Mexico cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in New Mexico have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For New Mexico debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A New Mexico debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In New Mexico, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

## Brunner Test in North Dakota [2026]: Eighth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/north-dakota.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in North Dakota [2026]: Eighth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for North Dakota residents.

Undue Hardship in North Dakota

North Dakota is in the 8th Circuit, which does NOT apply the Brunner test. Instead, the 8th Circuit uses a totality-of-the-circumstances test under Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003). Courts weigh past, present, and future financial resources, reasonable living expenses, and any other relevant facts - with no rigid three-prong structure.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A North Dakota debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the totality-of-the-circumstances framework described below.

The Eighth Circuit Framework

Does NOT apply Brunner. Uses the totality-of-the-circumstances test. Long v. Educational Credit Management Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003); ECMC v. Jesperson, 571 F.3d 775 (8th Cir. 2009). Structurally more debtor-friendly.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in North Dakota, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling North Dakota cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Private Student Loans and North Dakota - The McDaniel Question

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8)(B). Loans that were not used solely for "qualified higher education expenses" - including living expenses beyond the cost of attendance, bar study loans, test prep loans, and some direct-to-consumer private loans - may fall outside Section 523(a)(8)(B) entirely and be dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

For North Dakota debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in North Dakota have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For North Dakota debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A North Dakota debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Partial Discharge in North Dakota

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In North Dakota, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for North Dakota Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every North Dakota debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness - up to $17,500 for qualifying teachers in low-income schools after five years.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

North Dakota Legal Aid and Clinic Resources

Legal Services of North Dakota; 8th Circuit totality test.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in North Dakota can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope; dischargeable without undue-hardship showing.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative; the 8th Circuit rejected the rigid Brunner three-prong framework.

## Brunner Test in Ohio [2026]: Sixth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/ohio.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Ohio [2026]: Sixth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Ohio residents.

Undue Hardship in Ohio

Ohio is in the Sixth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding filed under Bankruptcy Rule 7001.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Ohio debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner three-prong framework described below.

The Sixth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner. In re Oyler, 397 F.3d 382 (6th Cir. 2005). Good-faith evaluated against repayment history and lifestyle choices.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in Ohio, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling Ohio cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in Ohio have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Ohio debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

In Ohio, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/oregon.html
