## Brunner Test in Pennsylvania [2026]: Third Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/pennsylvania.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Pennsylvania [2026]: Third Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Pennsylvania residents.

Undue Hardship in Pennsylvania

Pennsylvania is in the Third Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding filed under Bankruptcy Rule 7001.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Pennsylvania debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner three-prong framework described below.

The Third Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner. In re Faish, 72 F.3d 298 (3d Cir. 1995). Some bankruptcy courts in the circuit permit partial discharge using Saxman-style reasoning.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in Pennsylvania, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling Pennsylvania cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Private Student Loans and Pennsylvania - The McDaniel Question

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8)(B). Loans that were not used solely for "qualified higher education expenses" - including living expenses beyond the cost of attendance, bar study loans, test prep loans, and some direct-to-consumer private loans - may fall outside Section 523(a)(8)(B) entirely and be dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

For Pennsylvania debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in Pennsylvania have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For Pennsylvania debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Pennsylvania debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Pennsylvania Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student-loan adversary proceedings under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8) are filed inside an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Pennsylvania consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the universe of cases where an adversary could have been brought.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,513 bankruptcy cases from Pennsylvania's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7415n/an/a

Chapter 131,098n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Partial Discharge in Pennsylvania

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In Pennsylvania, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for Pennsylvania Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every Pennsylvania debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness - up to $17,500 for qualifying teachers in low-income schools after five years.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

Pennsylvania Legal Aid and Clinic Resources

Community Legal Services of Philadelphia; MidPenn Legal Services; 3rd Circuit Faish.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in Pennsylvania can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.

## Brunner Test in Rhode Island [2026]: First Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/rhode-island.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Rhode Island [2026]: First Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Rhode Island residents.

Undue Hardship in Rhode Island

Rhode Island is in the 1st Circuit, which blends Brunner with totality-of-the-circumstances flexibility. The three-prong framework supplies structure but courts retain equitable discretion on the "additional circumstances" prong.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Rhode Island debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the blended Brunner framework described below.

The First Circuit Framework

Blends Brunner with totality-of-circumstances flexibility. Bronsdon v. ECMC, 435 B.R. 791 (1st Cir. BAP 2010); In re Nash, 446 F.3d 188 (1st Cir. 2006). Partial discharge and equitable considerations are comparatively accessible.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in Rhode Island, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling Rhode Island cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Private Student Loans and Rhode Island - The McDaniel Question

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8)(B). Loans that were not used solely for "qualified higher education expenses" - including living expenses beyond the cost of attendance, bar study loans, test prep loans, and some direct-to-consumer private loans - may fall outside Section 523(a)(8)(B) entirely and be dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

For Rhode Island debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in Rhode Island have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For Rhode Island debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Rhode Island debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Partial Discharge in Rhode Island

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In Rhode Island, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for Rhode Island Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every Rhode Island debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

## Brunner Test in South Dakota [2026]: Eighth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/south-dakota.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in South Dakota [2026]: Eighth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for South Dakota residents.

Undue Hardship in South Dakota

South Dakota is in the 8th Circuit, which does NOT apply the Brunner test. Instead, the 8th Circuit uses a totality-of-the-circumstances test under Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003). Courts weigh past, present, and future financial resources, reasonable living expenses, and any other relevant facts - with no rigid three-prong structure.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A South Dakota debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the totality-of-the-circumstances framework described below.

The Eighth Circuit Framework

Does NOT apply Brunner. Uses the totality-of-the-circumstances test. Long v. Educational Credit Management Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003); ECMC v. Jesperson, 571 F.3d 775 (8th Cir. 2009). Structurally more debtor-friendly.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative; the 8th Circuit rejected the rigid Brunner three-prong framework.

## Brunner Test in Tennessee [2026]: Sixth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/tennessee.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Tennessee [2026]: Sixth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Tennessee residents.

Undue Hardship in Tennessee

Tennessee is in the Sixth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding filed under Bankruptcy Rule 7001.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Tennessee debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner three-prong framework described below.

The Sixth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner. In re Oyler, 397 F.3d 382 (6th Cir. 2005). Good-faith evaluated against repayment history and lifestyle choices.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in Tennessee, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling Tennessee cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Private Student Loans and Tennessee - The McDaniel Question

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8)(B). Loans that were not used solely for "qualified higher education expenses" - including living expenses beyond the cost of attendance, bar study loans, test prep loans, and some direct-to-consumer private loans - may fall outside Section 523(a)(8)(B) entirely and be dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

For Tennessee debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in Tennessee have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For Tennessee debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Tennessee debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Tennessee Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student-loan adversary proceedings under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8) are filed inside an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Tennessee consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the universe of cases where an adversary could have been brought.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,840 bankruptcy cases from Tennessee's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 758995.5%4.5%

Chapter 131,25117.3%82.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Partial Discharge in Tennessee

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In Tennessee, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for Tennessee Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every Tennessee debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness - up to $17,500 for qualifying teachers in low-income schools after five years.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

Tennessee Legal Aid and Clinic Resources

Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee; 6th Circuit Oyler.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in Tennessee can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.

The Fifth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner. In re Gerhardt, 348 F.3d 89 (5th Cir. 2003). Historically strict; Thomas (2019) narrowed "minimal standard of living" while reaffirming the basic framework.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

Foundational Caselaw

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope; dischargeable without undue-hardship showing.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative; the 8th Circuit rejected the rigid Brunner three-prong framework.

## Brunner Test in Virginia [2026]: Fourth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/virginia.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Virginia [2026]: Fourth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Virginia residents.

Undue Hardship in Virginia

Virginia is in the Fourth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding filed under Bankruptcy Rule 7001.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Virginia debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner three-prong framework described below.

The Fourth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner strictly. In re Frushour, 433 F.3d 393 (4th Cir. 2005). Good-faith inquiry expects documented IBR/IDR attempts and payment efforts.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in Virginia, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling Virginia cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Private Student Loans and Virginia - The McDaniel Question

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8)(B). Loans that were not used solely for "qualified higher education expenses" - including living expenses beyond the cost of attendance, bar study loans, test prep loans, and some direct-to-consumer private loans - may fall outside Section 523(a)(8)(B) entirely and be dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

For Virginia debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in Virginia have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For Virginia debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Virginia debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Virginia Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student-loan adversary proceedings under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8) are filed inside an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Virginia consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the universe of cases where an adversary could have been brought.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,064 bankruptcy cases from Virginia's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7514n/an/a

Chapter 1355071.2%28.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Partial Discharge in Virginia

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In Virginia, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for Virginia Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every Virginia debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness - up to $17,500 for qualifying teachers in low-income schools after five years.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

Virginia Legal Aid and Clinic Resources

Legal Aid Justice Center; Virginia Poverty Law Center; 4th Circuit Frushour.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in Virginia can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.

## Brunner Test in Washington [2026]: Ninth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/washington.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Washington [2026]: Ninth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Washington residents.

Undue Hardship in Washington

Washington is in the 9th Circuit, which applies Brunner with the Pena gloss (In re Pena, 155 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 1998)). Partial discharges are available and the DOJ/DOE November 2022 attestation guidance is well-integrated into practice.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Washington debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner with Pena gloss framework described below.

The Ninth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner with the Pena gloss. In re Pena, 155 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 1998). Partial discharges and DOJ/DOE Nov 2022 guidance well-integrated into practice.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Washington debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

In Washington, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in Wisconsin can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope; dischargeable without undue-hardship showing.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative; the 8th Circuit rejected the rigid Brunner three-prong framework.

## Brunner Test in Wyoming [2026]: Tenth Circuit Undue Hardship Application
Source: https://brunnertest.org/states/wyoming.html

← brunnertest.org home

Brunner Test in Wyoming [2026]: Tenth Circuit Undue Hardship Application

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Wyoming residents.

Undue Hardship in Wyoming

Wyoming is in the Tenth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding filed under Bankruptcy Rule 7001.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). A Wyoming debtor who wants them discharged must file an adversary proceeding inside the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the Brunner three-prong framework described below.

The Tenth Circuit Framework

Applies Brunner. In re Woodcock, 45 F.3d 363 (10th Cir. 1995). The McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) decision narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) - important for private loan dischargeability.

The Brunner three-prong test (where applicable) requires the debtor to prove by a preponderance of the evidence:

Minimal standard of living. The debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and their dependents if forced to repay the loans under current terms.

Persistence of hardship. Additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. The debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay - including enrollment in IDR plans, attempted forbearances, and demonstrated payment history where possible.

See the three-prong test in depth and totality-of-circumstances comparison.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (November 2022)

On November 17, 2022, the Department of Justice (Civil Division) and the Department of Education issued joint guidance streamlining federal student loan adversary proceedings. The guidance applies in every federal bankruptcy court, including those in Wyoming, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation framework:

The debtor completes a standardized attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation using objective criteria (below 225% of the federal poverty guideline, inability to repay projected for the future, demonstrated good-faith efforts).

If criteria are met, DOJ recommends not opposing discharge, either in full or in part.

The underlying Brunner or totality analysis is still applied by the bankruptcy judge, but with alignment between debtor and creditor.

The U.S. Trustee's office handling Wyoming cases processes attestations consistently with this guidance. See DOJ/DOE guidance deep-dive.

Private Student Loans and Wyoming - The McDaniel Question

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), narrowed what counts as a "qualified education loan" under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8)(B). Loans that were not used solely for "qualified higher education expenses" - including living expenses beyond the cost of attendance, bar study loans, test prep loans, and some direct-to-consumer private loans - may fall outside Section 523(a)(8)(B) entirely and be dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

For Wyoming debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans that exceeded the school-certified cost of attendance may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans are typically dischargeable under McDaniel/Campbell reasoning.

Mixed-use loans are fact-specific; the creditor bears the burden to prove qualified-loan status.

Even outside the 10th Circuit, bankruptcy courts in Wyoming have cited McDaniel persuasively. See recent case outcomes.

Income-Driven Repayment and the Good-Faith Prong

For Wyoming debtors in a Brunner-applying circuit (i.e., not the 8th), the good-faith prong is usually the hardest to meet. Courts expect evidence of:

Enrollment in (or attempted enrollment in) an income-driven repayment plan (SAVE/REPAYE, PAYE, IBR, or ICR).

Forbearances and deferments used when appropriate - but not as a substitute for actual repayment.

Communication with the loan servicer, including documented payment attempts.

Efforts to maximize income or minimize expenses where realistic.

A Wyoming debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly payment under SAVE. The point of showing IDR enrollment is not that it produced high payments - it is that the debtor tried. See good-faith requirement explained and persistent effort documentation.

Partial Discharge in Wyoming

Under In re Saxman, 325 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2003), and similar reasoning adopted in other circuits, bankruptcy courts may grant partial discharge where full discharge is not warranted but some reduction is equitable. In Wyoming, partial discharge is most accessible in the 1st, 7th, 9th, and (via totality) 8th Circuits; the 4th, 5th, and 6th Circuits treat it more skeptically.

Partial discharge options include: reducing principal, wiping out accrued interest, extending repayment terms, or discharging some loans in full while leaving others. See partial discharge in depth.

Alternatives for Wyoming Debtors

Before filing an adversary proceeding, every Wyoming debtor should check whether a non-bankruptcy path fits:

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge - administrative, no adversary needed. Available for federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans via SSA/VA/physician certification.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) - 120 qualifying payments while employed by a qualifying public-sector or nonprofit employer.

Teacher Loan Forgiveness - up to $17,500 for qualifying teachers in low-income schools after five years.

Borrower Defense to Repayment - full discharge where the school engaged in misconduct.

Closed School Discharge - full discharge where the school closed during enrollment or shortly after.

See alternatives to Brunner.

Wyoming Legal Aid and Clinic Resources

Legal Aid of Wyoming; 10th Circuit McDaniel.

Adversary proceedings typically cost $2,000-$6,000 in attorney fees beyond the base Chapter 7 or 13 representation. Legal aid, law school clinics, and pro bono panels in Wyoming can reduce or eliminate that cost for eligible debtors. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), all attorney fees connected to the case (including adversary fees) must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and are reviewable for reasonableness.
